design_detail: Six-session, double-blind, placebo-controlled, Latin-square balanced crossover in 12 men who used methamphetamine intravenously and were not dependent. Each received, about a week apart, single intravenous doses of d-methamphetamine 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg, l-methamphetamine 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg, racemic methamphetamine 0.5 mg/kg (0.25 mg/kg of each enantiomer) and saline placebo, each over 1 minute. Plasma was sampled to 48 hours and analysed with an enantioselective gas chromatography–mass spectrometry assay; cardiovascular, respiratory, temperature, subjective (verbal and visual analogue), mood-questionnaire and monetary-value measures were taken repeatedly over 48 hours.
can_establish: How the two methamphetamine enantiomers, given separately and as a 1:1 mixture, differ in plasma pharmacokinetics (AUC, peak, clearance, half-life, metabolite formation) and in acute cardiovascular and subjective effects, within the same people under double-blind, placebo-controlled conditions with a balanced order.
cannot_establish: What happens after repeated or sustained dosing, which is where the authors expect the enantiomers to differ most; effects by any other route (only intravenous was studied); effects in women (none were recruited) or in people who are dependent; and the health consequences of either isomer, since no outcome beyond acute physiology and ratings was measured.

sample.recruitment: Not described beyond the setting: a university drug-dependence research laboratory in San Francisco, with inpatient stays at a general clinical research centre (pp. 406–407).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Men aged 21–45 in good physical health by examination, laboratory tests and electrocardiogram, within 15% of ideal body weight, reporting intravenous methamphetamine use between once weekly and once or twice every 6 weeks, not dependent on methamphetamine, alcohol or other drugs by DSM-IV criteria and not seeking treatment. Excluded: significant medical or psychiatric illness, substance-use treatment in the last 12 months, current dependence on any drug except caffeine or nicotine, medications affecting the study or drug kinetics, and sensitivity to the study drugs. Hepatitis C and HIV status were not assessed (p. 406).
sample.demographics: 12 men; mean age 32.3 years (SD 7.4, range 23–43); mean weight 73.5 kg (SD 7.0, range 68.2–90.9); mean height 177.6 cm (SD 6.1, range 165–185); 9 white and 3 Black by self-report (p. 408). The paper states that although women were not excluded, none was recruited (p. 406).
sample.attrition: All 12 completed all six sessions; missing data accounted for less than 1% of values and were replaced by the group mean at that time point (pp. 407–408).
sample.selection_effects: Men only, not dependent, using intravenously as rarely as once every six weeks, healthy enough to pass a medical screen: a sample with some tolerance but far from the heaviest use, and the subjective ratings and monetary valuations come from people already experienced with this route.

exposure.measurement: Drug administered in the laboratory under double-blind conditions and measured directly: an enantioselective assay (chiral capillary column, trifluoroacetyl derivatives, deuterated internal standards) quantified d- and l-methamphetamine and d- and l-amphetamine in plasma, linear from 0.5 to 500 ng/mL with a limit of quantification of 1 ng/mL (pp. 406–407).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, each given once intravenously over 1 minute: d-methamphetamine 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg; l-methamphetamine 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg; racemic methamphetamine 0.5 mg/kg; placebo (saline). Doses were prepared by the investigational pharmacist from stock solutions of material obtained commercially and recrystallized in the authors' laboratory, with purity, identity and sterility established under an investigational new drug application; each aliquot was diluted to the same volume to preserve the blind (pp. 406–407).
exposure.polysubstance: Current dependence on any drug other than caffeine or nicotine was an exclusion; participants were asked to abstain from drugs and alcohol except caffeine and nicotine for 48 hours before admission, and urine toxicology at admission delayed a session if recent use was evident (pp. 406–407). Tobacco and caffeine use are not quantified.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: 48 hours' self-reported abstinence before each admission, checked by urine toxicology; sessions about one week apart, with 48 hours of inpatient observation after each dose (pp. 406–407).

comparison.controls: Saline placebo in the same participants, one of the six sessions; the enantiomers are also compared with each other and with the racemate within person.
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover with a Latin-square balanced order across the six conditions.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable: every comparison is within person against the same participant's placebo session.

outcomes.instruments: Non-compartmental pharmacokinetics (WinNonlin): AUC to the last measurable concentration and to infinity, peak concentration, terminal rate constant, half-life, systemic clearance and volume of distribution in the elimination phase; relative exposure as the ratio of d- to l-enantiomer AUC with 90% confidence intervals, judged against the 80–125% bioequivalence range. Pharmacodynamics: automated blood pressure and heart rate, rate-pressure product, manual respiratory rate, skin and tympanic temperature by thermocouple; verbal 0–100 intoxication rating; 0–100 visual analogue scales for any drug effect, good drug effect, drug liking, bad drug effect, intoxication and high; Profile of Mood States; Beck Depression Inventory; State-Trait Anxiety Inventory; Buss Aggression Scale; and a monetary value from $0 to $20 for the dose received (pp. 407–408).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard laboratory scales and validated questionnaires; the monetary-value measure is a laboratory analogue of drug valuation with no external norms.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Abuse liability' is inferred from positive subjective ratings and the monetary value participants assigned to the dose; no self-administration or choice procedure was used.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None at the family level: significance was set at P ≤ .05, with post-hoc Fisher least-significant-difference or Scheffé tests after a significant F. Table I reports ten pharmacokinetic parameters for each of six dosing conditions and Table II eighteen peak measures for each of six conditions, with pairwise comparisons against placebo and against three other conditions (pp. 407–408, 414).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind administration with identical injection volumes; blinding integrity was not tested, and participants experienced with intravenous methamphetamine may well have distinguished the active conditions from placebo.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table I gives means (SD) with 95% confidence intervals for every pharmacokinetic parameter. Half-life: d-methamphetamine 10.2 (SD 2.3), 10.3 (SD 2.6) and 10.7 (SD 2.6) h at 0.25 mg/kg, 0.5 mg/kg and in the racemate; l-methamphetamine 13.6 (SD 3.8), 13.3 (SD 3.5) and 15.0 (SD 4.6) h (overall P<.0001; at 0.5 mg/kg P = .0049). Clearance 0.257–0.266 L·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹ for the d-isomer and 0.188–0.221 for the l-isomer; volume of distribution 3.73–4.17 L/kg with no significant difference between isomers (P = .2206). Peak concentration 76.7 (SD 25.3) and 131.9 (SD 24.4) ng/mL for d-methamphetamine at the two doses, 65.4 (SD 18.1) and 125.9 (SD 30.7) for l-methamphetamine. Relative exposure (d/l AUC ratio): 0.910 (90% CI 0.837–0.983) at 0.25 mg/kg and 0.894 (0.821–0.967) at 0.5 mg/kg, against 0.679 (0.622–0.736) after the racemate, which falls outside the 80–125% range. Amphetamine formation differs sharply by isomer: amphetamine-to-methamphetamine AUC ratio 0.162–0.173 for the d-isomer and 0.029–0.038 for the l-isomer. Pharmacodynamics (Table II, mean peak change with SD): systolic pressure +34.5 (18.9) mm Hg after 0.5 mg/kg d-methamphetamine and +33.4 (17.8) after the racemate, against +19.5 (11.3) after 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine and +4.3 (9.9) after placebo; heart rate +13.5 (18.5), +18.7 (23.4), +10.7 (10.2) and +3.7 (9.8) beats/min; visual-analogue intoxication 46.0 (35.3), 24.7 (27.4), 30.3 (24.9) and 1.7 (4.7); drug liking 47.7 (35.1), 33.3 (28.7), 28.6 (24.8) and 2.1 (3.9); monetary value $14.60 (9.6), $10.70 (9.2), $11.30 (8.8) and $1.10 (2.4). No standardized effect sizes are given; the standard deviations are large relative to the means for most subjective measures.
analysis.covariates: None; repeated-measures ANOVA on change scores from pre-dose values, with dosing condition and time as within-subject factors.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; the study was conducted under investigational new drug application 58,189 with institutional review board approval (pp. 406–407).
analysis.selective_reporting: Time courses appear in figures without printed values; the Profile of Mood States, Beck Depression Inventory, State-Trait Anxiety Inventory and Buss Aggression Scale results are reported mainly as null findings; urinary excretion and p-hydroxylation, named in the limitations as important, were not examined.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. With 12 participants the pharmacokinetic contrasts are reasonably precise (the confidence intervals are printed), while the subjective contrasts have standard deviations close to or above their means and are much less precise.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The two enantiomers have similar volumes of distribution and broadly similar exposure when given separately, but l-methamphetamine is eliminated more slowly (half-life about 13–15 hours against 10–11 hours) and is converted to amphetamine about four to seven times less. After the racemate, exposure to the l-isomer exceeded exposure to the d-isomer. Acutely, doses containing d-methamphetamine raised blood pressure, heart rate and positive subjective ratings more and for longer (up to about 6 hours) than l-methamphetamine, whose effects returned to baseline by about 2–4 hours; the racemate behaved much like d-methamphetamine on most measures, and l-methamphetamine at 0.5 mg/kg was not inert.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine produced peak intoxication and drug-liking ratings "similar to" the same dose of d-methamphetamine, and prints the pairs (46.0 ± 35.3 versus 30.3 ± 24.9; 47.7 ± 35.1 versus 28.6 ± 24.8) in an order that reads as if the higher value were the l-isomer's. In Table II the higher value in each pair is the d-isomer's, and the Results state that 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine produced significantly smaller effects than 0.5 mg/kg d-methamphetamine on intoxication, any drug effect and drug liking (P<.0001) and than the racemate (P<.05). The conclusion that racemic methamphetamine would have an abuse liability comparable to d-methamphetamine is supported by these acute data in this sample, but it is a prediction about products and markets drawn from single intravenous doses in 12 non-dependent men, and the authors' own limitations section lists the single route, the narrow dose range, the single dose and the absence of repeated dosing (p. 418).

timeline.event: Smoked and intravenous pharmacokinetics of S-(+)-methamphetamine in 6 men: half-life 11.1–12.2 h, consistent with the d-isomer values here
Intranasal and smoked bioavailability study from the same San Francisco laboratory, sharing two authors: half-life about 10.7 h
Oral sustained-release dosing: half-life 9.3–11.1 h for the d-isomer, the form given in all these studies

replication.where_it_stands: This remains the only controlled human comparison of the methamphetamine enantiomers with a stereoselective assay; no independent replication was found in the sources read for this card. The d-isomer half-life agrees with three other laboratories, which supports the assay and the design; the l-isomer values and the racemate exposure finding rest on this study alone and should be labelled single-study.

funding.funder: Grants DA12521, DA18179 and DA12393 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health; carried out in part at the General Clinical Research Center, University of California, San Francisco, with NIH support (grant RR-00079). One author was supported in part by a Merck, Sharp & Dohme International Fellowship in Clinical Pharmacology, with two of the authors as US sponsors (p. 403).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflict of interest (p. 419).
funding.affiliations_note: Author affiliations include a pharmaceutical company (ALZA, Palo Alto) alongside the university laboratories, and the fellowship above is industry-funded. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results. The paper's framing question is the likely consequence of precursor regulation, a policy question, which is relevant to how its conclusions are worded (pp. 403–405, 417).

what_would_settle_it: A repeated-dosing crossover with the racemate and each enantiomer, with stereoselective plasma sampling long enough to measure accumulation of the l-isomer, including women, and with a self-administration or choice procedure rather than ratings alone, so that the prediction about the relative abuse liability of racemic and d-methamphetamine is tested on behaviour.

domains.domain: Randomization process (Latin-square allocation of the six conditions)
domains.note: A Latin-square balanced crossover is described, but the sequence generation and allocation concealment are not, and no period effect is reported.
Sessions about a week apart, which is more than ten half-lives for the d-isomer and about eight for the l-isomer; no methamphetamine was detectable before dosing (p. 408).

Double-blind with matched injection volumes, but blinding integrity was not assessed and the placebo and l-methamphetamine 0.25 mg/kg conditions were plainly less intoxicating, so participants experienced with the drug could probably tell the conditions apart.
All 12 completed all six sessions; under 1% of values were missing and were replaced by the group mean at that time point.
Stereoselective assay and automated cardiovascular measurement are objective (low); the subjective ratings and monetary valuations are self-reports whose blinding cannot be assumed (some concerns).

No protocol or pre-specified primary outcome; about forty outcomes with uncorrected pairwise tests; time courses only in figures; the abstract's description of the subjective comparison does not match Table II.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The design is the strongest among the pharmacokinetic studies read here: placebo-controlled, double-blind, balanced crossover, with an enantioselective assay and every participant receiving all six conditions, so the pharmacokinetic contrasts between isomers are internally valid. The concerns are the untested blind, the uncorrected multiplicity across many outcomes, and an abstract that describes the subjective comparison in a way its own table does not support. The source can be cited for the enantiomer differences in half-life, clearance, amphetamine formation and relative exposure after the racemate, and for the acute cardiovascular and subjective profile of single intravenous doses; it cannot be cited for repeated dosing, other routes, women, or for a market-level prediction about abuse liability.

key_findings.finding: The elimination half-life was shorter for d-methamphetamine than for l-methamphetamine in every condition: 10.2 h (SD 2.3), 10.3 (SD 2.6) and 10.7 (SD 2.6) against 13.6 (SD 3.8), 13.3 (SD 3.5) and 15.0 (SD 4.6) at 0.25 mg/kg, 0.5 mg/kg and within the racemate (P<.0001 overall; P = .0049 at 0.5 mg/kg).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetic results, penultimate paragraph of the section, the one beginning with the volume of distribution (p. 408, right column); Table I, t½ row (pp. 410–411)

key_findings.finding: Systemic clearance was higher for the d-isomer (0.257–0.266 L·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹) than for the l-isomer (0.188–0.221), while the volume of distribution was 3.73–4.17 L/kg and did not differ between isomers (P = .2206).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetic results, 1st–2nd paragraphs (p. 408, right column); Table I, CL and Vd rows (pp. 410–411)

key_findings.finding: Given separately, the two isomers produced nearly equal exposure: d/l AUC ratio 0.910 (90% CI 0.837–0.983) at 0.25 mg/kg and 0.894 (0.821–0.967) at 0.5 mg/kg. After the racemate the ratio fell to 0.679 (90% CI 0.622–0.736), outside the 80–125% range, that is, exposure to the l-isomer exceeded exposure to the d-isomer within the same injection.
key_findings.note: The Results describe this as the l-isomer AUC being '30% greater' than the d-isomer's; from the printed ratio the correct statement is that the d-isomer's AUC was about 32% smaller, or the l-isomer's about 47% greater (editors' calculation, 1/0.679 = 1.47).

key_findings.finding: Both AUC and peak concentration roughly doubled from 0.25 to 0.5 mg/kg for each isomer, consistent with linear kinetics over this range; peak concentrations were 76.7 (SD 25.3) and 131.9 (SD 24.4) ng/mL for d-methamphetamine and 65.4 (SD 18.1) and 125.9 (SD 30.7) for l-methamphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetic results, 3rd paragraph (left column, p. 408); Table I, AUC and Cmax rows (pp. 410–411)

key_findings.finding: Conversion to amphetamine is strongly stereoselective: the amphetamine-to-methamphetamine AUC ratio was 0.162–0.173 for the d-isomer and 0.029–0.038 for the l-isomer, a four- to sevenfold difference, and amphetamine peaked 12–18 h after dosing with a half-life of 32.5–64.6 h.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetic results, last paragraph (p. 408, right column); Table I, amphetamine rows (pp. 410–411)

key_findings.finding: Peak increases in systolic blood pressure were 34.5 mm Hg (SD 18.9) after 0.5 mg/kg d-methamphetamine and 33.4 (SD 17.8) after the racemate, against 19.5 (SD 11.3) after 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine and 4.3 (SD 9.9) after placebo; peak heart-rate increases were 13.5 (SD 18.5), 18.7 (SD 23.4), 10.7 (SD 10.2) and 3.7 (SD 9.8) beats/min.
key_findings.note: Heart-rate changes were not ordered by dose: the 0.25 mg/kg d-methamphetamine condition gave the second-largest mean (18.0, SD 11.7), larger than the 0.5 mg/kg condition.

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular effects peaked about 5–15 minutes after the 1-minute infusion in every condition; after l-methamphetamine they returned to baseline within 2–4 hours, while after conditions containing d-methamphetamine they persisted for up to 6 hours.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamic measures › Physiologic measures, paragraph beginning 'phetamine produced greater and longer-lasting cardiovascular effects'; Figure 4 (p. 413)

key_findings.finding: Peak visual-analogue intoxication was 46.0 (SD 35.3) after 0.5 mg/kg d-methamphetamine, 36.7 (SD 25.6) after 0.25 mg/kg d-methamphetamine, 30.3 (SD 24.9) after 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine, 24.7 (SD 27.4) after the racemate, 14.6 (SD 20.3) after 0.25 mg/kg l-methamphetamine and 1.7 (SD 4.7) after placebo; peak drug liking for the same conditions was 47.7, 38.9, 28.6, 33.3, 14.9 and 2.1, so the order differs from intoxication: the racemate was rated above 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Table II, visual analog scales block

key_findings.finding: At 0.5 mg/kg, l-methamphetamine produced significantly smaller effects than the same dose of d-methamphetamine on intoxication, any drug effect and drug liking (P<.0001) and smaller than the racemate (P<.05); its subjective effects approached baseline at about 3 hours, while conditions containing d-methamphetamine remained intoxicating for up to 6 hours. The 0.25 mg/kg l-methamphetamine condition did not differ from placebo on any subjective measure.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamic measures › Subjective measures, 1st–2nd paragraphs (p. 410); Figure 5 (p. 415)

key_findings.finding: Participants valued all doses containing d-methamphetamine and the higher l-methamphetamine dose at a mean of $10.70 to $14.60 per dose, against $1.10 for placebo and $4.60 for 0.25 mg/kg l-methamphetamine; monetary value was the one subjective measure on which 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine matched the d-methamphetamine conditions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamic measures › Subjective measures, 2nd–3rd paragraphs (p. 410); Table II, Monetary value row (p. 414); Figure 6 (p. 416)

key_findings.finding: All doses were tolerated: no serious adverse events occurred and no clinically significant changes in electrocardiography, examination, vital signs or laboratory tests were observed. The authors state that the responses obtained were 25–50% of the maximum they considered safe.
key_findings.locator: Results › Tolerability of methamphetamine (p. 408); Discussion › Study limitations (p. 418)

key_findings.finding: The authors list their own limitations: only the intravenous route, only two doses over a narrow range, only single doses with no repeated-dosing arm, and no examination of p-hydroxylation or urinary excretion.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports the systolic blood-pressure changes (33.4 ± 17.8 and 34.5 ± 18.9 against 19.5 ± 11.3) in units of beats per minute; Table II and the Results give them in mm Hg.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader quoting the abstract would attribute a blood-pressure change to heart rate; the mm Hg values in Table II are the correct ones.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine as producing peak intoxication and drug-liking ratings similar to the same dose of d-methamphetamine, listing the pairs 46.0 ± 35.3 versus 30.3 ± 24.9 and 47.7 ± 35.1 versus 28.6 ± 24.8 in an order that attributes the larger value to l-methamphetamine. Table II shows the larger value in each pair belongs to d-methamphetamine, although without a significant difference between the two 0.5 mg/kg conditions in peak intoxication or drug liking, and the Results report the l-isomer's effects as significantly smaller (P<.0001) in the analysis across time.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's pairs are in reversed order; its description of the peak ratings as similar is consistent with Table II (no significant peak difference), but the across-time comparison favours d-methamphetamine and the l-isomer's effects are shorter-lived, so the Results and Table II should be used instead.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that after the racemate the AUC for l-methamphetamine was 30% greater than that for d-methamphetamine, while the printed mean ratio of 0.679 corresponds to the d-isomer being about 32% smaller, or the l-isomer about 47% greater (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Two incompatible percentages for the same comparison circulate within the paper (the abstract's 'd 30% smaller' is the one consistent with the ratio); the ratio with its confidence interval should be cited rather than either percentage.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table I, the peak amphetamine concentration after the racemate (d-enantiomer) is printed as 4.9 ± 1.8 with a 95% confidence interval of 4.9–7.6; a mean cannot coincide with the lower bound of its own symmetric interval, and the interval's midpoint is about 6.3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the mean or the interval is mistyped; the amphetamine peak for that condition cannot be read from the table with confidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give the amphetamine half-life range as 33.0 to 65.0 hours, while Table I lists 32.5, 64.6, 33.5, 43.6 and 40.6 hours for the five conditions in which it could be estimated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor rounding mismatch between text and table.

reporting_issues.issue: The legends of Figures 4, 5 and 6 state that mean data are shown for N = 12 except for the 0.5 mg/kg d- and l-methamphetamine conditions, for which means with standard deviations are given.
reporting_issues.consequence: Dispersion is displayed for two of the six conditions only, so the figures cannot be used to compare variability across conditions.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table I, the amphetamine AUC0–t after 0.25 mg/kg l-methamphetamine is printed as 32.1 ± 21.6 with a 95% confidence interval of 13.4–45.8; the interval's midpoint is 29.6, not the mean, and its half-width (16.2) is wider than the 13.7 implied by the SD with 12 participants (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the mean or the interval is mistyped, as for the amphetamine peak after the racemate; the cell cannot be read from the table with confidence.
